items.title: 2.3 Graph of the Square Root Function

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The basic square root function is \(y = \sqrt{x}\). It is defined only for \(x \ge 0\) (the square root of a negative number is not real), and \(\sqrt{x}\) itself is never negative. Its graph starts at the origin and rises, more and more slowly: \(\sqrt{0} = 0\), \(\sqrt{1} = 1\), \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), \(\sqrt{9} = 3\).
In \(y = 2\sqrt{x} + 1\) the factor \(2\) doubles every value (a vertical stretch), and the \(+1\) moves the whole graph one unit up. So the graph starts at \((0, 1)\) instead of \((0, 0)\).

blocks.title: Example 10
steps:
Given: the square root function \(y = 2\sqrt{x} + 1\).
To find: its domain and range, a table of values and its graph.
Method: find which \(x\) are allowed (domain) and which \(y\) come out (range), then make a table of values, plot the points and join them with a smooth curve.

Step 1: Domain
Clearly the domain of \(y = 2\sqrt{x} + 1\) is \(x \ge 0\), as the square root of a negative number is not a real number.
Why: \(\sqrt{x}\) is a real number only when \(x\) is zero or positive.

Step 2: Range
The book prints: the range of \(y = 2\sqrt{x} + 1\) is \(y \ge 0\), as the square root of a non-negative number is also non-negative.
Working it out: \(\sqrt{x} \ge 0\) for every \(x\) in the domain, so
\[2\sqrt{x} \ge 0\]
\[2\sqrt{x} + 1 \ge 1\]
and \(y = 1\) is reached at \(x = 0\). So the range is \(y \ge 1\), i.e. \([1, \infty)\).
Why: the reason the book gives (a square root is never negative) is right, but the \(+1\) lifts every value by 1, so the smallest value of \(y\) is \(1\), not \(0\).

Step 3: Table of values
\[x = 0:\ y = 2\sqrt{0} + 1 = 1\]
\[x = 1:\ y = 2(1) + 1 = 3\]
\[x = 2:\ y = 2(1.414) + 1 \approx 3.8\]
\[x = 4:\ y = 2(2) + 1 = 5\]
\[x = 9:\ y = 2(3) + 1 = 7\]
The other values in the table below are found the same way and rounded to one decimal place.
Why: perfect squares \(0, 1, 4, 9\) give exact values; the others need a calculator.

Step 4: Plot and join
Plot the points of the table and join them with a smooth curve starting at \((0, 1)\) (see the table and graph below).
Why: the graph starts at \((0, 1)\) because no \(x < 0\) is allowed; it keeps rising, but more and more slowly.

Check:
The lowest point of the graph is \((0, 1)\), so no \(y\) below \(1\) occurs: range \(y \ge 1\). For example \(y = 0\) would need \(2\sqrt{x} = -1\), which is impossible.
blocks.answer: Domain: \(x \ge 0\); range: \(y \ge 1\). The graph is the curve through the table points, starting at \((0, 1)\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book states that the range of \(y = 2\sqrt{x} + 1\) is \(y \ge 0\). Since \(2\sqrt{x} \ge 0\), we get \(2\sqrt{x} + 1 \ge 1\); the correct range is \(y \ge 1\), i.e. \([1, \infty)\). The book's own table and graph start at \(y = 1\).
Table values and the graph of the function are given below:

blocks.caption: Table (as printed in the book): values of y = 2√x + 1, to one decimal place

blocks.alt: Graph of y = 2 times the square root of x, plus 1, for x from 0 to 11, with the y-axis marked 1 to 7. The curve starts at (0, 1) and rises ever more slowly through the table points (1, 3), (4, 5) and (9, 7) up to about (10, 7.3).
blocks.caption: Figure: graph of y = 2√x + 1, starting at (0, 1) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(y = \sqrt{x}\): domain \(x \ge 0\), range \(y \ge 0\).
2. \(y = a\sqrt{x} + c\) with \(a > 0\): domain \(x \ge 0\), range \(y \ge c\); the graph starts at \((0, c)\).
3. Use perfect squares (0, 1, 4, 9, ...) for exact points; round the others.
4. The curve is smooth and rises more slowly as \(x\) grows.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Copying the range of \(\sqrt{x}\) without the shift: for \(2\sqrt{x} + 1\) the range is \(y \ge 1\), not \(y \ge 0\).
2. Plotting points for negative \(x\): they are not in the domain.
3. Joining the points with straight segments or drawing the curve to the left of the \(y\)-axis.
